questions.q: Why is the CSV loaded into Excel as a Power Query Table rather than pasted as plain values?
options: Plain pasted values cannot be summed with SUMIFS
A Power Query import can be refreshed later against a newer export with Data → Refresh All, without rebuilding the PivotTable or formulas on top of it
Power Query is required before any PivotTable can be created
Pasted values take up more disk space than a Table
questions.explain: Using Power Query keeps the import refreshable, which matters for a workbook that will be reused each QBR cycle.

questions.q: What does the PivotTable built in this lesson summarize, and how does it compare to Power BI's Regional Drill-Down page?
options: It summarizes sales by TerritoryName and CategoryName — the same kind of breakdown Power BI gives Executives, but built independently from a flat CSV instead of a modeled star schema
It summarizes sales reasons using the bridge table from Chapter 2
It is functionally identical to Power BI's model, sharing the same live connection
It only shows a single grand total with no breakdown at all
questions.explain: The PivotTable gives a territory/category view using nothing but Excel's own summarization, built completely independently of the Power BI model.

questions.q: What are the two criteria used in the quarter-total SUMIFS formula in this lesson?
options: Data[OrderDate] >= July 1, 2013 AND Data[OrderDate] <= October 1, 2013
Data[TerritoryName] = "Pacific" AND Data[CategoryName] = "Bikes"
Data[OrderQty] > 0 AND Data[LineTotal] > 0
Data[OrderDate] = July 1, 2013 only
questions.explain: The formula sums LineTotal where OrderDate is on or after July 1, 2013 and on or before October 1, 2013 — a lower and upper date bound.

questions.q: Why does this lesson note that the SUMIFS formula "looks completely reasonable" even though something about it will later need closer examination?
options: Because the formula contains a syntax error Excel would reject outright

Because every criterion compiles, references real columns, and produces a number — nothing about it looks alarming on a quick glance, which is exactly why it has to be checked against independent numbers rather than trusted on sight
Because SUMIFS cannot actually handle date criteria in any version of Excel
Because the PivotTable and the SUMIFS formula will always disagree by definition
questions.explain: A formula not looking wrong is not the same as a formula being right — this lesson deliberately sets up the need for Lesson 22's cross-check.

questions.q: Why does the SUMIFS formula wrap its date boundaries in DATE(2013,7,1) instead of writing the dates as plain text?
options: DATE() has no real effect and is purely cosmetic
Wrapping dates in DATE() ensures Excel compares them as real date values rather than as text strings
DATE() is required syntax for any SUMIFS formula regardless of the criteria
Using DATE() automatically fixes any boundary errors in the formula
questions.explain: DATE() produces an actual date value Excel can compare numerically against Data[OrderDate], rather than relying on text comparison, which could behave unpredictably.
